column2: Here's a puzzle about two games of chance. Each one, played on its own, slowly loses money. Can switching between them ever make money?
Before guessing, let's learn the games properly, with one player and real rounds. The player starts with seven dollars.
Every round, the player tosses a coin. Heads wins a dollar, and tails loses one.
Game A uses a single bent coin. It lands heads forty-nine and a half percent of the time, just under half.
Watch a few rounds. The money wanders up and down, and here it even climbs. A handful of tosses can't tell you whether a game wins or loses.
So think in averages instead. In a hundred rounds you expect forty-nine and a half wins and fifty and a half losses.
On average, how much does the player lose per round?
One dollar per hundred rounds, which is a cent a round. Tiny, but it never stops.
Here's one simulated player, playing game A for a hundred thousand rounds. The path wobbles, but drifts down, about a thousand dollars below where it started.
That's losing slowly. Luck decides any short stretch, and the cent a round decides the long run.
Game B has two coins and a rule for choosing between them. Before every round, the player counts their dollars and asks one question.
Does the count divide by three? Arrange the dollars in rows of three and look at what's left over.
Seven dollars make two rows with one left over. Eight leave two over. Nine fill three rows exactly, with nothing left over. That leftover is the remainder, and it's always zero, one or two.
When the remainder is zero, the player must toss the bad coin. It lands heads only nine and a half percent of the time.
Any other remainder, and the player tosses the good coin. It lands heads seventy-four and a half percent of the time.
Try one yourself. With ten dollars, which coin does the player toss?
The good coin. Ten dollars make three rows with one left over, so the remainder is one.
Now say the good coin wins twice in a row from seven. Seven becomes eight, and eight becomes nine. The count divides by three, and out comes the bad coin.
So how often does the player meet the bad coin? Two counts in every three don't divide by three.
If the good coin really got two rounds in three, game B would win fifty-two point eight percent of them.
So does game B win or lose in the long run?
It loses. Here's the same player, a hundred thousand rounds of game B. The money drifts down again, though more slowly than in game A.
And look at how often the bad coin came out. Not a third of the rounds, but more than thirty-eight percent.
Those extra rounds with the bad coin are what sink game B. Why they happen is the heart of this video.
Now the switching. Before every round, the player flips a fair coin. Heads means play game A, and tails means play game B. Call this the mix.
Here's why the mix looks hopeless. Take two ordinary coins that both lose, one landing heads forty-nine percent of the time and one forty-eight.
Choosing between them with a fair coin works exactly like one coin that lands heads halfway between, forty-eight and a half percent. Two losers mix into a loser.
Averaging the games seems to agree. Game A loses a cent a round and game B a little under a cent, so halfway between should still be a loss.
So when the player plays the mix, do they win or lose in the long run?
They win. Here's the same player, a hundred thousand rounds of the mix. The money climbs, ending well over a thousand dollars above where it started.
Nothing about the coins changed, so something else did. In game B, the player stood on a multiple of three more than thirty-eight percent of the time. In the mix, more often or less?
Less. In the mix, the player stood on a multiple of three only about thirty-four and a half percent of the time, much closer to a third.
That's the puzzle, and it's real. Two games that each lose, mixed by a fair coin, make a game that wins just over one and a half cents a round.
The catch is hidden in game B's rule, the part that reads your money. To find it, we need a better picture of where the player stands, and then a crowd of players.
Game B only ever looks at the remainder, so let's track just that. Draw three corners, one for each remainder, zero, one and two.
The player's seven dollars leave one over, so the player stands at corner one. A win moves them one corner forward, to corner two.
From corner two, where does one more win take the player?
Around to corner zero. Eight dollars plus one is nine, and nine leaves nothing over. A loss always moves one corner back.
Now write game B on the triangle. From corner zero, the bad coin, forward nine and a half percent of the time. From corners one and two, the good coin, forward seventy-four and a half percent.
Game A is the same from every corner, forward forty-nine and a half percent, back fifty and a half.
Whether you hold six dollars or six hundred, game B plays the same way at corner zero. So what decides game B is how often you stand at each corner.
If you play only game A for a long time, what share of the rounds do you spend at corner zero?
One third. Game A treats every corner alike, so in the long run the corners share the rounds equally. The player's game A run spent thirty-three and a half percent there.
Game B does not treat its corners alike. Its run spent more than thirty-eight percent at corner zero, and that's what we need to explain.
To see why, make the numbers rounder for a while. Each coin in these games is a round percentage with half a point shaved off. Put the half point back.
Game A becomes a fair coin, so on average it neither wins nor loses. Game B gets a ten percent coin at corner zero and a seventy-five percent coin everywhere else.
These round coins are our worked example, not the published games. With equal thirds at every corner, B would now win fifty-three point three percent of its rounds.
So is it really a third each? One player's path is full of luck. To see past it, imagine twenty-six copies of the player, all starting at corner zero and all playing game B.
Let the crowd split exactly by the coins' chances. After one round, where is most of the crowd?
At corner two. A tenth of the crowd moves forward, and nine tenths fall back to corner two.
The next round, three quarters of corner two win their way around to zero. Every player is always somewhere, so the total stays twenty-six while the crowd sloshes between corners.
Watch the share at corner zero, where the bad coin waits. It swings wildly at first, then steadies above a third.
Round after round the sloshing dies down, and the crowd settles at ten players on corner zero, four on corner one and twelve on corner two. Not a third each.
Check that this crowd really stays put. At corner zero, ten players toss the bad coin. One wins and moves forward. Nine lose and drop back to corner two.
At corner one, four players toss the good coin. Three win and move on to corner two, and one falls back to zero.
At corner two, twelve players. Nine win and wrap around to zero, and three fall back to one.
Now let everyone move at once. How many players land on each corner?
Corner zero gets one plus nine, ten. Corner one gets one plus three, four. Corner two gets nine plus three, twelve. Every player moved, and the crowd looks exactly the same.
Count the winners. One, three and nine make thirteen, exactly half of twenty-six. Without the half point, game B is perfectly fair.
Now look at where the crowd sits. Ten of twenty-six is thirty-eight and a half percent, more than a third.
Those extra rounds at corner zero, with the bad coin, cancel the good coin's advantage exactly.
Why does corner zero collect extra players? Follow one who has just arrived there. Where is that player most likely to be one round later?
At corner two, nine times in ten. The bad coin knocks them back. And from corner two, the good coin usually wins, which carries them forward, around to zero again.
So most of the good coin's wins at corner two just bring the player back to zero, where the bad coin waits.
That's the trap in game B. The good coin wins often, but its wins keep getting spent on climbing back to a multiple of three.
One change removes the trap. Let a die choose B's coin instead of your money. A one or a two means the bad coin, anything else the good coin.
Now the bad coin really does get one round in three, wherever you stand, and this game wins fifty-three point three percent of the time.
Same two coins. Only the rule that picks between them changed. Reading your money is what drags game B from fifty-three point three percent down to exactly half.
Each corner's long-run share of the rounds is called its weight. For game B, the weights are five thirteenths, two thirteenths and six thirteenths.
Now mix the games, as the player did. Before every round, a fair coin decides whether you play A or B.
On the triangle, every arrow becomes an average. At corner zero, half the time it's A's fifty percent, half the time B's ten percent. So forward thirty percent in all.
At corners one and two, halfway between fifty and seventy-five, forward sixty-two and a half percent.
Start the mix from game B's settled crowd, ten, four and twelve. Which way will the crowd shift?
Off corner zero. Round by round, corner zero's share falls from thirty-eight point five percent to thirty-four point six, and corner one's climbs from fifteen point four to twenty-five point four.
Game A's coin ignores the corners, so its rounds keep stirring the crowd toward equal thirds. That shift of weight off corner zero is where the winning comes from.
Split the mix's rounds into A rounds and B rounds. The A rounds win exactly half the time, at every corner, so they can't be where the winning comes from.
Game B's chance of winning depends on just one number, its share of rounds at corner zero. Every round it spends there swaps a seventy-five percent coin for a ten percent one.
At a third, B wins fifty-three point three percent. At game B's own thirty-eight point five, exactly half.
Inside the mix, B's rounds spend thirty-four point six percent at corner zero. So what do they win?
Fifty-two point five percent. Averaged with the A rounds' fifty, the mix wins fifty-one point three percent of all its rounds.
On average, that's a gain of just over two and a half cents a round.
So game A's rounds only break even. They move the crowd off the bad corner, and game B's good coin does the winning.
Remember the first count, with a third of the rounds at each corner? The mix pushes the crowd most of the way back to it.
Now shave the half point off every coin again, back to the coins Harmer and Abbott published, the ones the player used.
Game A slips from fair to losing a cent a round.
Game B's crowd barely moves. Corner zero still holds thirty-eight point four percent of its rounds, and with the weaker coins that's now too many. B loses a little under a cent a round.
The mix had an edge of just over two and a half cents a round. Does it survive the handicap?
It does. The half point costs the mix about one cent a round, and the edge was bigger than that. The mix still wins just over one and a half cents a round.
Inside the mix, corner zero still holds only thirty-four and a half percent, so B's rounds still win fifty-two point one percent.
That's every number from the opening. A loses a cent a round, B a little under a cent, and the coin-flip mix of the two wins.
Harmer and Abbott named the effect after its discoverer, Juan Parrondo. Their paper, in Nature in nineteen ninety-nine, is a single page.
There's a test that decides any game like these, without finding where the crowd settles. It starts from how a settled crowd moves around the triangle.

Go back to the round numbers, and take the mix's crowd, scaled up to one thousand four hundred eighteen players so every count is whole. Across each edge, twelve more players go forward than come back.
Every forward step wins a dollar and every backward step loses one. So how many dollars does this crowd gain each round?
Thirty-six, twelve for each of the three edges. That's seven hundred twenty-seven winners against six hundred ninety-one losers.
In any settled crowd, every edge carries the same net flow, and the gain per round is three times it. A game is fair exactly when that flow is zero.
When is the net flow zero? Then every edge balances on its own, the players going forward across it equal to the players coming back.
Multiply the three balances together. The weights appear once on each side and cancel.
What's left compares the two ways around. Winning three times in a row, all the way around the triangle, is exactly as likely as losing three times in a row the other way.
For game B without the half point, a tenth times three quarters times three quarters, against nine tenths times a quarter times a quarter. Both come to nine over one hundred sixty. Balanced, so fair.

For the mix, the forward product is thirty percent times sixty-two and a half percent twice over. The backward product is seventy percent times thirty-seven and a half percent twice over. Which is bigger?
Forward, seventy-five over six hundred forty against sixty-three. When the forward product is bigger, the crowd turns forward and the game wins. When it's smaller, the game loses.
With the half point shaved off, game B's forward product drops below its backward one, and the mix's stays above. Two products per game decide A, B and the mix.
Switching helped here for one reason. Game B's coin reads your money, and game A's rounds move your money around.
Remember the two ordinary coins. Mix two losing ordinary coins and you always get a losing coin, with the average chance.
Even these two games don't win under every schedule. What happens if you strictly alternate, A, then B, then A, then B?

It loses, about two thirds of a cent a round. The random mix wins, and the rigid alternation of the same two games loses. Two A's, then two B's, the pattern in the original paper, wins about one and a half cents.

The share of A matters too. With A on only one round in twenty, the mix loses. With A on nine rounds in ten, it loses again. The mix wins only when A's share is between about seven and eighty-five percent.
So there is no general rule that switching between losing games wins. It works here, with these coins and these schedules, because one game reads the money and the other moves it.
Look back at the player's run of game B. After a thousand rounds it was sixteen dollars ahead, even though game B loses.
Just over one and a half cents a round is an average over the very long run. Over a hundred rounds, luck is much bigger than that.
Start a crowd at zero dollars and let everyone play the mix for a hundred rounds. Just over half finish ahead, and about two in five finish behind.
After a thousand rounds, what share of the crowd is ahead?
A little more than two in three. The average gain grows in step with the number of rounds, while the spread of luck grows only like its square root.
In the long run, a player's average per round settles on just over one and a half cents, with probability one. Over a thousand rounds of game A or game B alone, most players end up behind.
These are invented games. What they teach is about chances that depend on where you stand, and none of it is advice about real money.
Back to the puzzle. Game A loses a cent a round, wherever the player stands.
Game B loses because its crowd piles up at corner zero, where the bad coin waits.
Flip a fair coin between them, and game A's rounds push the crowd off corner zero. Game B's rounds, played from better corners, now win more than half the time.
One last puzzle, to solve from the picture. Play game B only when the count divides by three, and game A at every other count.
Does this way of switching win or lose?
It loses, and badly, about twenty-eight cents a round. Every coin around the triangle now favors going back.
Swap the roles, A at corner zero and B everywhere else, and the same two games win about thirty-one cents a round. What decides it is where each coin gets tossed.
For any game drawn on this triangle, the verdict is that comparison. Win, win, win one way round against lose, lose, lose the other. Whichever is more likely is the way the money flows.
To look further, search for Parrondo's paradox, Markov chains, and the flashing ratchet that Harmer and Abbott compared it to.
